# Best ACT Question Bank 2026: Free, Paid, and Official


## TLDR


An ACT question bank is a searchable library of practice questions organized by section, topic, and difficulty. The best ACT question bank matches the Enhanced ACT format, explains every answer thoroughly, tracks your timing and accuracy, and helps you drill weak skills between full-length practice tests. Official ACT materials offer the highest realism, but third-party question banks add the volume and analytics needed for targeted improvement.


## What Is an ACT Question Bank?


An ACT question bank is a collection of ACT-style practice questions you can filter by section (English, Math, Reading, Science), topic, difficulty level, or question type. Unlike a worksheet or a PDF of random problems, a proper question bank lets you choose exactly what to practice, see detailed explanations, and track your performance over time.


Think of it this way: a question bank is a gym with individual weight machines, while a full-length practice test is a marathon. Both serve a purpose, but they train different things.


A strong question bank includes five components:


- Questions organized by skill and difficulty
- Correct answer explanations that cover why wrong answers are wrong, too
- Filters so you can isolate weak topics
- Timing data so you know if speed or knowledge is the problem
- Progress tracking to show whether you are improving


[Practice ACT questions by topic](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/question-bank) to see what a structured question bank workflow looks like in action.


## Question Bank vs. Practice Test: They Are Not the Same Thing


Students often confuse these two tools, and the confusion costs them time.


A **practice test** simulates the full ACT exam under real timing. It measures where you stand right now. It builds stamina and reveals pacing issues. But it is not great for fixing specific weaknesses because the questions come in a fixed order across mixed topics.


A **question bank** is for targeted reps. If you bombed punctuation questions on your last practice test, a question bank lets you do 30 punctuation questions in a row, review every mistake, and then move to the next weak area.


PrepScholar makes a similar distinction, warning that practice tests are not a cure-all and that students should spend more time[reviewing mistakes between tests](https://blog.prepscholar.com/complete-official-act-practice-tests-free-links) than simply taking more exams. The winning strategy uses both tools: question banks for daily skill building, practice tests for periodic readiness checks.


## What Makes the Best ACT Question Bank?


Most comparison pages just list resources by question count. That is not enough. A question bank with 6,000 questions is useless if the questions do not match the current ACT or the explanations are shallow.


Here are the seven criteria that actually matter.


### 1. Enhanced ACT Format Fidelity


This is non-negotiable in 2026. The Enhanced ACT changed question counts, timing, answer choices, and scoring. Math now has 45 questions in 50 minutes with four answer choices instead of the old 60 questions with five choices. The Composite score is based on English, Math, and Reading only. Science is optional for many test-takers. Any question bank still built around the legacy format will mislead your pacing and expectations.


For a full breakdown of the current structure, see this guide on[ACT format, sections, and timing](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/act-test-format-sections-timing-scoring) .


### 2. Explanation Quality


The best ACT question bank does not just tell you the right answer. It explains why the right answer works, why each wrong answer is tempting, what skill was tested, and how to solve the problem faster next time. If a question bank does not help you understand why you missed a question, it is a question list, not a prep tool.


### 3. Topic and Difficulty Filters


You should be able to drill specific weak areas: comma rules, function notation, inference questions, data interpretation. Without filters, you waste time on skills you have already mastered.


### 4. Timing Data


Practitioners on Reddit consistently ask for this feature. One r/ACT user specifically requested a question bank with “time spent on each question” alongside explanations. A student who answers correctly in untimed mode may still miss under[ACT pacing pressure](https://www.reddit.com/r/ACT/comments/1sf72oi/act_prep_websites/) . Timing data separates knowledge gaps from speed gaps.


### 5. Analytics and Error Review


A good bank shows your accuracy by section and topic, highlights repeat mistakes, and helps you revisit missed questions. Without this, you are practicing blind.


### 6. Official vs. Unofficial Question Balance


Official ACT questions are the gold standard because they reflect the test maker’s actual style and difficulty calibration. But official materials are limited. The smart approach preserves official tests for checkpoint assessments and uses a quality question bank for daily targeted drills.


### 7. Cost and Access


Some banks are free. Others run $49 to $300. The right choice depends on what you need: more volume, better explanations, mobile access, analytics, or AI-guided study. Start free, pay when free resources stop meeting your needs.


## The Enhanced ACT: What Your Question Bank Must Reflect


If your question bank does not account for these changes, your practice will not transfer to test day.


The Enhanced ACT sections break down like this, according to[ACT’s official examinee information](https://www.act.org/content/act/en/products-and-services/state-and-district-solutions/act-info-for-examinees.html) :


Section Questions Time Time per Question


English 50 35 min 42 sec


Math 45 50 min 67 sec


Reading 36 40 min 67 sec


Science 40 40 min 60 sec


Writing 1 essay 40 min N/A


Key changes from the legacy ACT:


- **Fewer questions, more time per question.** The old ACT had 215 questions across four sections. The Enhanced ACT has 171.
- **Math uses four answer choices** instead of five. This changes guessing odds and elimination strategy.
- **Science is optional** for most national test-takers. It became optional for national online testing in April 2025 and expanded from there. Students who take Science still receive a Science score, and potentially a STEM score if they also attempted Math.
- **Composite score** is now calculated from English, Math, and Reading only, not Science. The 1 to 36 scale remains unchanged.


For students wondering how many questions they will actually face, see[how many questions are on the ACT](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-many-questions-are-on-the-act) .


## Best ACT Question Banks by Use Case


There is no single best ACT question bank for everyone. The right choice depends on your budget, timeline, and what you need most.


### Best for Official Realism: ACT.org


ACT offers[free official practice tests](https://www.act.org/content/act/en/products-and-services/the-act/test-preparation/free-act-test-prep.html) with real questions. The current page lists Practice Tests 1 through 4 with both digital and paper options. These are the highest-fidelity practice available because they come directly from the test maker.


The limitation: official materials are finite. You will run through them quickly if you use them for daily drilling instead of reserving them for checkpoint assessments.


The[Official ACT Prep Guide 2026-2027](https://www.act.org/content/act/en/products-and-services/the-act/test-preparation/the-official-guide.html) adds four authentic full-length tests and subject guides with access to an online question bank.


### Best Free Question Bank: OnePrep


OnePrep claims over 1,300 free ACT questions across English, Math, Reading, and Science. The bank organizes questions by section, topic, and difficulty with instant explanations and progress tracking. For students on a tight budget who need volume beyond official tests, this is a strong starting point.


### Best Paid Question Bank for Explanations: UWorld


UWorld claims over 2,500 ACT-style questions with custom quizzes by topic, difficulty, and question type. Their selling point is explanation depth: detailed breakdowns for every correct and incorrect answer choice. The QBank starts at $99.


### Best for Full-Length Simulations: Test Innovators


Test Innovators claims 10 full-length Enhanced ACT practice tests alongside thousands of targeted questions. If you need more realistic full-test simulations beyond the four official ones, this fills the gap.


### Best for Classroom Volume: Albert


Albert lists ACT access at $196 total (or $49 per subject) with over 6,400 practice questions, 44 topic review quizzes, and 11 practice exams. This scale makes it useful for tutors and teachers who need large libraries for multiple students.


### Best Budget Course Option: Magoosh


Magoosh claims official ACT questions created under license from ACT, plus an AI tutor, video lessons, and mobile apps. The full course starts at $129, positioning it between free resources and premium platforms.


### Best Free Explanation Supplement: Piqosity


Piqosity provides detailed answer explanations for the official ACT practice tests that ACT releases for free. If you are working through official tests and want deeper walkthroughs than the scoring key provides, Piqosity fills that gap.

The workflow moves from identifying weaknesses to drilling them to measuring progress, all in one place.

## How to Use an ACT Question Bank Without Wasting Time


Buying or signing up for a question bank is not prep. Using it well is. Here is a five-step framework.


### Step 1: Start With a Diagnostic


Take an official ACT section or a diagnostic test to identify your baseline weaknesses. Do not start drilling random topics. Students who skip this step often practice skills they have already mastered while ignoring the areas that would move their score fastest.


### Step 2: Drill One Weak Skill at a Time


Pick your weakest topic from the diagnostic. Examples:


- English: comma splices and semicolons
- Math: function notation or coordinate geometry
- Reading: inference questions or vocabulary in context
- Science: experiment comparison or graph interpretation


Do 15 to 25 focused questions on that single skill. Review every miss before moving on.


### Step 3: Review Every Mistake


This is where score gains actually happen. For each missed question, write down:


- What skill the question tested
- Why the correct answer works
- Why your answer was tempting
- What you would do differently next time


This is called an error log, and it is the single most underused tool in ACT prep.


### Step 4: Mix Topics Under Time Pressure


After drilling individual skills, do timed mixed sets. This prevents the artificial ease that comes from knowing every question tests the same concept. It also builds the mental flexibility you need on test day.


### Step 5: Use Full-Length Tests as Checkpoints


Take a[full-length ACT practice test](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/practice-tests) every one to two weeks. These measure whether your targeted practice is translating into overall score improvement.


For a detailed week-by-week approach, check out the[ACT study plan guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/act-study-plan-step-by-step-guide) .


## Should You Use Old ACT Questions for the Enhanced ACT?


Yes, but with clear limits.


Old ACT questions are still useful for content practice. Grammar rules have not changed. Algebra is still algebra. Reading comprehension passages still test inference, main idea, and function. The underlying skills transfer.


But old tests will mislead you on pacing and format. The Enhanced ACT has different question counts, different timing per section, four-choice Math instead of five, and a different Composite calculation. Practicing exclusively with legacy materials means test day will feel unfamiliar.


Community tutors on Reddit echo this point. In one thread about finding Enhanced ACT practice, a commenter noted that legacy tests remain useful for content but that[English is the biggest adjustment](https://www.reddit.com/r/ACT/comments/1vy6zs9/where_can_i_find_more_enhanced_practice_tests/) because the Enhanced ACT includes question types like tone and redundancy more explicitly.


The practical rule: use old ACT questions for topic-specific drills. Use Enhanced ACT materials for timed full-section and full-test practice.


## ACT Question Bank Strategy by Section


Not all sections reward the same approach. Here is what to prioritize in each.


### ACT English


Focus your question bank drilling on punctuation, sentence structure, verb agreement, pronoun clarity, concision, organization, and style/tone. English is the most rule-driven section, which makes it the most trainable through targeted reps.


### ACT Math


Community analysis matters here. One practitioner on Reddit manually tagged 307 questions from Enhanced ACT Math tests and found that roughly 44% were word problems, about one-fourth included a diagram or graph, and about half required only one core math skill. This is community analysis rather than official ACT data, but it highlights something important: practice translating words into equations and interpreting visuals, not just solving clean algebraic expressions.


For formulas you should know cold, see the[ACT Math formulas guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/act-math-formulas-essential-guide) .


### ACT Reading


Volume alone will not help here. Reading question banks should train you to identify wrong-answer traps: unsupported inferences, answers that are too broad or too narrow, wrong tone, and out-of-scope claims. One test prep practitioner on LinkedIn advises students to “read for purpose,” identify what the author is doing in each paragraph, and eliminate answers that add ideas the passage never supports.


### ACT Science


Even though Science is optional for many students, it is still worth preparing if your school or district requires it, if your target colleges value it, or if you want a STEM score. A Science question bank should train data-table and graph scanning, experiment comparison, and variable identification. The skill is reading data efficiently, not memorizing biology or chemistry facts.


## Free vs. Paid ACT Question Banks


Start free. Official ACT practice tests and free question banks from platforms like OnePrep and Manhattan Review (which claims 740 free questions) can carry you a long way, especially if you review mistakes carefully.


Pay when you hit one of these walls:


- You have exhausted the free question supply in your weak areas
- You need better explanations than the answer key provides
- You want analytics to track accuracy by topic over time
- You need timing data to separate speed problems from knowledge problems
- You want mobile access for studying between classes or on a commute
- You need a personalized plan instead of self-directed exploration


ACT reports that students who initially score between 13 and 29 improve their Composite by an average of[one point when retesting](https://www.act.org/content/act/en/students-and-parents/high-school-success/testing-advice-for-the-act/reasons-to-retest.html) . Gains increase for students who use review tools like ACT My Answer Key. The point: targeted review, not just more questions, drives improvement.


## How Many Questions Should You Practice?


There is no magic number. A focused set of 20 to 30 questions with deep review is almost always better than rushing through 100 questions without understanding mistakes.


General guidance by prep intensity:


- **Light prep (6+ weeks out):** 15 to 25 targeted questions per session, 3 to 4 sessions per week
- **Moderate prep (3 to 6 weeks out):** 25 to 40 questions per session plus thorough error review
- **Final month:** Daily targeted drills plus one full official section or practice test each week
- **High scorers (30+):** Fewer random questions, more hard mixed sets with detailed review


Students aiming for competitive scores can check[what counts as a good ACT score](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/what-is-a-good-act-score-percentiles-ranges) to calibrate their targets. For reference, a 30 Composite places you at the[94th percentile](https://www.act.org/content/act/en/products-and-services/the-act/scores/national-ranks.html) , and a 32 reaches the 97th.


## Common Mistakes Students Make With ACT Question Banks


### Doing Questions Without Reviewing Misses


This is the most common and most costly mistake. Grinding through hundreds of questions without analyzing errors is like running laps without ever fixing your stride. The review is where improvement happens.


### Using Only Unofficial Questions


Third-party questions are useful for volume and targeted drilling. But some differ from official ACT style in subtle ways, and practitioners on Reddit regularly warn against relying on them exclusively. One commenter advised students not to spend time on third-party practice tests and to use ACT prep material because it is the most accurate. Use official tests as your reality check.


### Ignoring Timing


A student who gets questions right in untimed mode but struggles under pressure has a pacing problem, not a knowledge problem. Always include timed drills in your practice routine.


### Using Old Materials as If Nothing Changed


The Enhanced ACT is structurally different from the pre-2025 ACT. Old questions can support content learning, but relying on them exclusively will leave you unprepared for the current format’s timing and structure.


### Skipping Science Without Checking Requirements


Science is optional in many contexts, but not all. ACT says colleges decide individually whether to require Science or Writing. Check your target schools before deciding to skip Science prep entirely.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the best ACT question bank?


It depends on your needs. Official ACT materials are best for realism. UWorld is strong for paid explanations and analytics. OnePrep is a solid free option. Miyagi Labs combines a diagnostic, question bank, AI tutor, practice exams, score predictor, and analytics into one guided prep workflow.


### Does ACT have an official question bank?


ACT offers free official practice tests (currently Practice Tests 1 through 4), subject-specific sample questions, and paid prep books. The Official ACT Prep Guide 2026-2027 includes four authentic full-length tests, and the subject guides include access to an online question bank.


### Are free ACT question banks enough?


Free banks can be enough for students who review carefully and use official tests as checkpoints. Paid banks become worth it when you need more questions in weak areas, deeper explanations, timing data, analytics, or a personalized study plan.


### Can I use old ACT questions for the Enhanced ACT?


Yes for content practice, particularly grammar, algebra, geometry, and reading comprehension. No as your only format simulation. The Enhanced ACT changed timing, question counts, Math answer choices, Science optionality, and Composite scoring.


### How many ACT practice questions should I do per day?


A focused set of 20 to 30 questions with thorough review is generally more productive than rushing through 100 questions. Quality of review matters more than quantity of questions completed.


### Is ACT Science still worth practicing?


Yes if your school or district requires it, if your target colleges value it, or if you want a Science or STEM score on your report. ACT says students who take Science receive a Science score, and those who also attempt Math may receive a STEM score.


### What should an ACT question bank explanation include?


A good explanation covers four things: why the correct answer is right, why each wrong answer is wrong, what skill the question tested, and how to solve the problem more efficiently next time.


### Is a question bank better than full-length practice tests?


Neither replaces the other. Full-length tests measure readiness and build stamina. Question banks build targeted skills and fix specific weaknesses. The best prep routine uses both.
